subject: PE & Wellbeing
source: National Curriculum (Physical Education); UK Chief Medical Officers' physical activity guidelines. Drive PE folder reviewed (TSS Long-Term PE Plan: fitness, fair play, leadership, resilience) and adapted to at-home, no-equipment, no-contact lessons.

lessons.title: Principles of training: FITT and progression
objectives: Explain Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type (FITT)
Apply FITT to a simple plan

keywords.def: Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type: ways to plan training
gradually increasing the demand on the body
training matched to the activity you want to improve
fitness lost when you stop training

starter: Bismillah. Name the five health-related components.

teach.heading: Safety first
bullets: Warm up and cool down every time
Stop and tell an adult if you feel pain
teach.note: Read this slide aloud every lesson. Parents are asked to confirm their child is well enough to take part and to tell the school about any medical condition (e.g. asthma: inhaler within reach). No contact activities in any TGA online PE lesson.

teach.heading: What is FITT?
bullets: Time and Type: how long, what kind
teach.note: Give an example: jogging on the spot 3 times a week, 20 minutes, moderate. Ask pupils to fill in a FITT table.

teach.heading: Progressive overload
bullets: Make training slightly harder over time
teach.note: Misconception: do as much as possible each time. Increase by only a small amount at a time.

teach.heading: Specificity and reversibility
bullets: Train what you want to improve
teach.note: Ask: how would you train for stamina? For flexibility? Discuss sensible maintenance.

teach.heading: Apply it
teach.note: Pupils write a four-week plan: week 1 vs week 4. Teacher checks that progression is gradual.

independent: Fill in a FITT table for a stamina plan.
Explain one way to progress a plan.
exit: Write a four-week plan for improving muscular endurance using FITT.
Explain how you will apply progressive overload.
lessons.send: Try the first week of your plan and note what you did.

lessons.title: Flexibility: dynamic and static stretching

keywords.def: holding a stretch still for 15 to 30 seconds
moving a joint through its range with control
how far a joint can move

starter: Give an example of a static stretch.

teach.heading: Safety first
bullets: Stretch to mild tension, not pain
teach.note: Read this slide aloud every lesson. Parents are asked to confirm their child is well enough to take part and to tell the school about any medical condition (e.g. asthma: inhaler within reach). No contact activities in any TGA online PE lesson.

teach.heading: Two types of stretch
teach.note: Pupils try one of each. Misconception: static stretching alone is a warm-up; a pulse raiser is needed first.

teach.heading: Dynamic routine
bullets: Gentle leg swings holding a wall
teach.note: Keep movements controlled; avoid big swings.

teach.heading: Static routine
teach.note: Hold 20 seconds each. Breathe out as you ease into the stretch.

teach.heading: Why flexibility matters
teach.note: Link to sitting for long periods in online lessons: stand and stretch regularly.

practice: How long should a static stretch be held?
independent: Perform four dynamic stretches with 10 reps.
Hold four static stretches for 20 seconds.
exit: Create a 5-minute mobility routine for sitting at a desk.
homework: Give one difference between static and dynamic stretching.
When should you do static stretching?
lessons.send: Do your mobility routine after each lesson day this week.
